documentation.range: Atlantic Mackerel are restricted to the North Atlantic Ocean and adjacent seas. In the western Atlantic, they are present from Labrador to Cape Lookout, USA. In the eastern Atlantic, they are present from Iceland to Mauritania, including the southwestern Baltic Sea, the Mediterranean and Black seas. They are widespread in the Mediterranean basin (Sinovčič 2001, Zardoya et al. 2004, Karachle 2017, Collette and Graves 2019).
documentation.population:
There are two main populations, Northwest Atlantic and Northeast Atlantic, with little or no interchange. The distribution of haplotypes between eastern and western Atlantic samples indicate that the two populations do not share a common gene pool (Scoles et al.1998). The range of the Northwest population of Atlantic Mackerel extends from North Carolina north to Canada but although there are two spawning groups (O’Brien et al. 1993), the population is currently managed as a single stock jointly by NOAA for the United States and DFO for Canada. From 1968 to 2008, the distribution of this stock shifted about 250 km to the north and east (Overholtz et al. 2011, Collette and Graves 2019). A separate stock assessment is conducted by ICES for the eastern population. The Mediterranean and Black Sea stocks are not well defined in terms of population, even if some studies hypothesised the existence of a subpopulation in the Adriatic Sea (Meneghesso et al. 2013, Papetti et al. 2013).

The world catch declined from about 1.1 million mt. tonnes in 1975 to about 610,000 mt. tonnes in 1981 (FAO 1983). The northeast Atlantic fishery grew rapidly from 1964 on, owing to the development of the Norwegian purse-seine fishery, reaching a peak catch of 934,000 tons in 1967. The catch decreased, falling to 340,000 tons by 1970 (Collette and Graves 2019). Catches have exceeded 500,000 t almost every year since 1980, 750,000 t since around 2010 and 1 million t from 2014 to 2018. However, considerable underreporting is suspected to have occurred between 1980 and 1999 (ICES 2020). In the western Atlantic, total catch increased from 7,353 mt in 1960 to a maximum of 432,608 mt in 1973. Total catch averaged approximately 30,000 mt from 1978–1983 and then increased to a peak of 86,423 mt in 1990. Average total catch was approximately 35,000 mt from 1992–2001, there was a peak of 112,425 mt in 2006 and there has been a decline in catch since then. Total catch has averaged 13,558 mt since 2011. In 2016, it was 15,316 mt (NOAA 2018). Catches in the Mediterranean Sea and Black Sea are only partly reported to GFCM and some data are suspected to include also the Atlantic Chub Mackerel and the Chub Mackerel.

World catch shows a generally increasing trend from 2009 to 2018, when the total was 1,046,660 t (FAO 2020).

Eastern Atlantic
The Northeast Atlantic population is currently considered to comprise three main unit stocks (Southern, Western and North Sea), with variable proportions of these three mixing in the northerly feeding grounds but this excludes the Mediterranean spawners (Jansen et al. 2013). Genetic data suggests population differentiation among the three Northeast spawning stocks and management as three stocks instead of a single stock even though there is no structuring among shoals of individuals outside of the spawning season (Nesbø et al. 2000). The Southern Stock, about 0.4 million tons, spawns in Spanish and Portuguese waters, and the Western Stock, about 2.5 million tons, spawns in the Bay of Biscay and northwards around Ireland and west/northwest of the UK (Collette and Graves 2019) The eastern Mediterranean populations (Greece, Italy) are separated genetically from the western Mediterranean stock that forms a panmictic unit with eastern Atlantic populations (Zardoya et al. 2004, Collette and Graves 2019). Our knowledge of the species’ distribution in the Mediterranean sea is limited and fragmented (Giannoulaki et al. 2017).

The third component, the North Sea Stock, has been reduced from about 4 million tons in 1960 to only about 0.1 million tons (Nesbø et al. 2000; Collette and Graves, 2019). This stock spawns in the North Sea and Skagerrak. Although the North Sea spawners form to some extent a discrete unit from the other ones, commercial catches cannot be allocated to individual stocks, and therefore assessments are undertaken for the combined stock (ICES 2006).

According to the latest (2020) stock assessment report for the Northeast Atlantic stock, the spawning-stock biomass (SSB) was increasing from 2007 onwards, with a peak in 2014, and has been decreasing since then. It has, however, stayed above MSY Btrigger since 2008. There has been a decrease in fishing mortality (F) since 2003, and F has been below FMSY since 2016. Large year classes have occurred in succession since 2001 and year classes have been above average since 2011 (ICES 2020).

There are no stock assessments for the Mediterranean Sea. However, Atlantic Mackerel were much more abundant in catches (peaks to around 23,000 mt) before 1965 and over the last 20 years, the catch has fluctuated between 5,000 and 15,000 mt with recent years showing higher landings. Catches have shown a marked decline over the last 40 years in the Adriatic Sea along with a decline in maximum age from 8 to 3 years and size from 42 to 36 cm TL (Sinovčič 2001, Meneghesso et al. 2013, Papetti et al. 2013, Collette and Graves 2019).

Western Atlantic
The northwest Atlantic stock is currently overfished and overfishing was occurring in 2019, the terminal year of the most recent assessment. Except for the mid-1980s and the early-2000s, when the SSB trend was temporarily increasing, there was a dramatic decline in SSB, from peak of approximately 1.1 million mt in 1972, to 15,319 mt in 2014. Since then, SSB increased to 42,862 mt in 2019 (NOAA 2021) but this was substantially less than had been projected for 2019. The U.S. assessment accounts for fish off both the U.S. and Canada. Otolith chemical and shape signatures suggest that the NW Atlantic stock should be regarded as two distinct population-units, northern and southern, for fisheries management purposes (Moura et al. 2020). A Canadian assessment that focuses on northern contingent fish has observed similar declines (DFO 2021).

North Atlantic (total)
Based on a generation length between 3.5 and 6.5 years (Western and Eastern stocks respectively), changes in population size can be measured over a period of 11–20 years. Two methods were used to estimate the changes. In the first method ("method 1"), the change was calculated based on the linear percent change in population size over the three generation lengths using 3-year averages for the endpoints. In the second method ("method 2"), and to account for non-linear trends, the average annual percent change in population size over the time period for which data are available was calculated, and then used to estimate the change in population size over the last three generation lengths, assuming an exponential decline.

In the Eastern stock, using method 1, SSB is estimated to have increased by 43% over 11 years (2009–2020) and 72% over 20 years (2000–2020). Using method 2, SSB is estimated to have increased by 2% over the last 11 years, and 4% over the last 20 years. The time period for which data was available was 1980–2020 (ICES 2020 and corresponding data retrieved from the ICES Stock Assessment Database).

In the Western stock, based on visual inspection of spawning stock estimates from 1968 to 2016, SSB between 1996 and 2016 (20 years) has fluctuated, with a high greater than ~ 250,000 mt around 2001/2002 and the aforementioned low of ~17,000 mt in 2012 (NOAA 2018).
documentation.habitats:
Atlantic Mackerel are pelagic and oceanodromous, mainly diurnal, and most abundant in cold and temperate shelf areas. They form large schools near the surface. They overwinter in deeper waters but move closer to shore in spring when water temperatures range between 11° and 14°C. The Northwest Atlantic stock migrates great distances on a seasonal basis. They are sensitive to changes in temperature, preferring water warmer than 5°C. Atlantic Mackerel fall prey to all the larger predaceous sea animals. Whales and porpoises, sharks and bony fishes such as tunas, bonito, Bluefish, and Striped Bass all take a heavy toll. Spiny Dogfish, Atlantic Cod, and Silver Hake are among the most important fish predators in the western North Atlantic (Bowman et al. 2000).

Atlantic Mackerel have two methods of feeding, either by filtering smaller pelagic organisms from the water using their gill rakers or by selecting individual animals by sight and then swallowing them whole. Practically all floating animals that are neither too large nor too small regularly serve to nourish them. Their diet changes markedly during growth, switching from copepods, amphipods, and larval fishes to larger prey such as squids and larger fishes like hakes. First-feeding larvae (3.5 mm) feed on phytoplankton (Peterson and Ausubel 1984). The diet of 4.5 mm larvae consists of larval crustaceans. Larvae larger than 6.5 mm are cannibalistic. In addition to conspecifics, larvae prey on other larval fishes such as Yellowtail Flounder, Silver Hake, and Redfish on the Scotian Shelf (Fortier and Villeneuve 1995). Young fish depend more and more upon larger food as they grow. Adults continue to feed on the same prey as juveniles but their diet includes a wider array of organisms and larger prey items. Euphausiid, pandalid, and crangonid shrimps are common prey; chaetognaths, larvaceans, pelagic polychaetes and the larvae of many different marine species have been identified from stomachs. Analysis of stomach contents of 3,617 Atlantic Mackerel collected from off the northeastern United States showed that the type of prey eaten varies enormously depending upon the year, the season, and the area (Bowman et al. 2000).

Until the mid-2000s, the feeding grounds of the Northeast population of Atlantic Mackerel were mostly limited to the North Sea and the Norwegian Sea. They have been extending their summer feeding distribution north and west, including around Iceland, since around 2006 (Óskarsson et al. 2016). The prey group that weighed most around Iceland was copepods, ranging from 70–80% of their diet. Euphausiids and hyperiid amphipods were also important, making the combined crustacean diet weight range from 70-99% of the total diet, like the diet of the co-occurring herring. Fishes, such as sandeel and capelin were also a significant part of the diet in some areas. In the North Aegean Sea of Greece, Atlantic Mackerel feed largely on fishes, particularly anchovies and sardines whereas the co-occurring Atlantic Chub Mackerel feed largely on fish larvae and crustaceans (Karachle 2017, Collette and Graves 2019).

Spawning of Atlantic Mackerel in the Northwest Atlantic occurs from April to August and progresses from south to north as surface waters warm and the fish migrate (Sette 1943). There are two spawning contingents. The southern contingent spawns from April to July in the Mid-Atlantic Bight and the northern contingent spawns in the southern Gulf of St. Lawrence in June and July (O’Brien et al. 1993). The mean peak of spawning in the southwestern Gulf of St. Lawrence is July 1 coinciding with the maximum abundance of summer plankton (Ware 1977). Most spawn in the shoreward half of the continental shelf although some spawning extends to the shelf edge and beyond. Atlantic Mackerel do not begin spawning until the water has warmed to about 8°C with the chief production of eggs taking place at temperatures of 9–14°C. Median lengths at maturity for females and males from the northeast coast of the United States were 25.7 and 26.0 cm FL, respectively (O’Brien et al. 1993). Median age at maturity was 1.9 years for both sexes. Batch fecundity estimates for fish between 31 and 44 cm FL ranged from 285,000 to 1,980,000 eggs in the Middle Atlantic Bight (Morse 1980). There are potentially 5–7 batches of eggs that could be spawned by an individual female.

Maturity estimated for Northeast Atlantic Mackerel indicate that more than half are mature at age 2, with 100% maturity at age 7 (Skagen 1989), although 90% of fish in the North Sea reach maturity at age 2 (ICES Fact Sheet). The generation length is estimated at 6.9 years (Collette and Graves 2019). The spawning distribution has shifted northward in the last three decades probably in response to global sea warming (Bruge et al. 2016, Astthorsson et al. 2012).

For the Western stock longevity is estimated to be about 12 years (Gregoire 1993), and for the Eastern stock longevity is estimated to be 18 years (Villamor et al. 2001). Generation length is therefore conservatively estimated to be about 3.5 years in the Western stock and 6.5 years in the Eastern stock (Collette et al. 2011). Disparities in longevity between stocks may valid, or may be due to differences in methods of age determination, environmental factors, and/or response to fishing pressure over time.

Age determination based on counting annual growth rings on otoliths of fish from the west coast of Portugal found ages between 0 and 15 years for fish with a length range of 16–49 cm (Costa et al. 2017). Maximum longevity is estimated to be 17 years (Collette and Graves 2019).

In the Mediterranean, knowledge of spawning mainly comes from the Adriatic Sea (Giannoulaki et al. 2017). They migrate in the autumn-winter from the northern portion to the central portion to reach a single central spawning ground in winter, mainly from January to March (Meneghesso et al. 2013, Papetti et al. 2013). Absolute fecundity of the largest females (31.7 cm) in the Adriatic was 190,000 oocytes (Meneghesso et al. 2013). Juveniles were most likely to be present on the continental shelf in the Mediterranean at a depth of less than 130 m combined with upwelling as well as in deeper waters when combined with downwelling (Giannoulaki et al. 2017). Atlantic Mackerel eggs generally float in the surface water layer above the thermocline or in the upper 10–15 m (Berrien 1975).

Atlantic Mackerel can reach a total length of 70 cm and a weight of 3.2 kg (Navarro et al. 2012) although fish greater than 50 cm are uncommon. The IGFA all-tackle game fish record is of a 3 lb., 8 oz. (1.6 kg) fish caught off L’Ampolla, Spain in August 2015 (IGFA 2022).
documentation.threats:
Atlantic Mackerel have high commercial importance in the Northwest Atlantic, the Northeast Atlantic, and the Mediterranean Sea. It is also an important recreational species, fished with hook and line.

In the northeast Atlantic stock, Climate change may affect the distribution of this species, with possible movement towards the north, making it available for exploitation by additional nations.  An expansion of habitat seems to be taking place in Iceland but it is not yet known if contraction will occur in the southern part (Collette and Graves 2019).
documentation.measures:
The first global assessment of the Atlantic Mackerel was Least Concern (Collette et al. 2011). The Red List assessment for the Atlantic Mackerel in Italy was assessed as Vulnerable (Relini et al. 2017). Several eastern Atlantic countries have minimum landing sizes for this species: EU (18 cm), Ukraine (15 cm), Türkiye (20 cm), Bulgaria (22 cm), Romania (23 cm).

ICES advises that any agreed total allowable catch (TAC) should cover all areas where Northeast Atlantic Mackerel are fished. The agreed management plan (F between 0.2 and 0.22) would imply catches between 527 000 t and 572 000 t in 2010. The SSB is expected to remain stable in 2011 for a catch in this range. ICES further advises that the existing measures to protect the North Sea spawning component remain in place. These include: areas restricted to fishing, seasonal closures, and minimum landing size (30 cm in North Sea and 20 cm in Skagerrak). In June 2009, an agreement was concluded between contracting parties to the Coastal States on mackerel banning high grading, discarding, and slipping from pelagic fisheries targeting mackerel, horse mackerel, and herring beginning in January 2010 (STECF 2009).

In 2020, ICES advised that catches in 2021 should be no more than 852,284 tonnes when the MSY approach is applied. Existing management measures to ensure the protection of the North Sea component include no mackerel fishing in divisions 3.a and 4.b-c except for Norway. Here, a limited amount of the TAC can be fished in Division 3.a. Other measures are no mackerel fishing in Division 4.a from 15 February to 31 July; and a 30 cm minimum conservation reference size (ICES 2020).

Western Atlantic stock: Canada closed their directed commercial and bait fisheries in 2022 to increase the chance of stock growth. The Canadian recreational fishery has a 20-fish per person limit and a 26.8 cm size limit (size tied to maturity parameters) but is believed to be a small component of historical catch. The U.S. implemented an emergency action to reduce quotas in 2022 while a revised rebuilding plan is developed – the emergency action was set to allow no more than 12,170 MT of combined U.S. and Canadian catch, but due to the Canadian closure, low early 2022 U.S. mackerel catch, and Atlantic herring restrictions that limit late-season Atlantic mackerel catch, combined Canadian and U.S. Atlantic mackerel catch should be less than 6,000 MT in 2022. A revised U.S. rebuilding plan will be implemented in January 2023, and by using more pessimistic assumptions about expected recruitment should help continue rebuilding. The U.S. rebuilding plan and associated quotas account for both U.S. and Canadian catch.
documentation.use_trade: This species is an important commercial and recreational fish (Collette and Graves, 2019).
documentation.rationale: This species occurs in the North Atlantic and is caught in commercial and recreational fisheries. There has been no overall decline in the spawning stock biomass of the larger northeast Atlantic stock over the last 11–20 years (three generation lengths). This species is therefore listed as Least Concern. However, spawning stock biomass has been decreasing since 2015. There have also been no stock assessments for the Mediterranean Sea, although catch, maximum age and size have all been declining in the Adriatic Sea. In the western Atlantic, the stock is overfished and overfishing is occurring.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Some authors have placed the other three species of the genus Scomber in a separate genus, Pneumatophorus, based on their possession of a swim bladder that is absent in the Atlantic Mackerel, but all four species are currently included in Scomber.
